edits.chapter_key: the persian who was dead and revived
edits.body_md:
إن أفضل الحسنات إحياء الأموات — I must keep this Arabic verbatim.

Let me produce the polished prose directly.

As for the doctrines of the righteous and the manners of those who seek the truth: it has reached us that a certain man among the people of Persia was afflicted by the calamity of ignorance. He was a man of keen and retentive heart, of sound intellect, and of a learning he had cultivated in himself; yet ignorance held sway over him in the very knowledge already described, for it had overtaken him early and he had grown up in the midst of it. And so he faltered in the heat of his thirst, taking the shimmer of the mirage for the whiteness of water, until, when he came to it, he found nothing of it there — and he found Allah waiting for him, and there his account was settled. Then Allah honored his resting-place and lifted from him the veil that had covered him. He found him astray and guided him, found him destitute and made him rich with knowledge. By that grace bestowed upon him he became one of the scholars of the Mount (Tur, الطور) and one who dwells at the Frequented House (Bayt al-Mamur, البيت المعمور).

When his guidance was complete and he had attained the utmost of his hope, it fell to him as a duty to give thanks to his Maker and to labor his way toward his Lord. He had heard from his father a saying that was to him as the soul is to the body:

إن أفضل الحسنات إحياء الأموات

"The best of good deeds is the reviving of the dead."

So he said to himself: "I was dead and He revived me, ignorant and He taught me. I was not the first to be ignorant, that I should be the one to outstrip all people to knowledge, nor am I the last, that teaching should come to an end with me. It is a binding obligation upon me to be one who gives thanks for this blessing, discharging this trust to those who come after me just as it was discharged to me by those who came before. For this matter has its origin with Allah, and it reached me only through a long chain of intermediary causes — the first conveying it to the second, and the second to the third, until it came down from the highest assembly to the creatures who are the people of this world. Then the veil was torn and the doors were forced, one after another, until at last it reached me. Am I, then, its endpoint and its final limit? No. Those who carried it and kept faith with the trust in it have the prior claim to the gains and the merits. And if their gains are not mine to lean upon, then I am only the one who was gained for them through their labor. Their merit does not excuse me from labor of my own; I remain as poor in my need to seek knowledge through action as once I was poor in my need to seek knowledge at all." This he said within himself, and he understood that what was owed by him was the very likeness of what had been owed to him, and that the end of his affair, in the final reckoning, was as its beginning.

So he set out, leaving his family and his wealth behind, toward his Lord — answering His call, praying for the good, and summoning others to the obligation, that there might become due to him the same thanksgiving that had become due from him. He took to journeying through the lands, passing among the peoples of the non-Arabs and the tribes of the Arabs, searching faces and putting questions, yet finding none to answer him and meeting no fellow seeker, until he reached the farthest bounds of the island (al-Jazira (الجزيرة)). He entered one of its cities at an hour when its people were heedless. And as he was calling the signs to mind and studying the marks, he caught sight of a company of the people of that land quarreling over religion without guidance and plunging headlong into the depths of their own caprice. So he sat down a little apart, withdrawn from them, listening to their words and observing them closely to see which among them held to the soundest way.

edits.chapter_key: the five shares and the long road to the shaykh
edits.body_md:
Praise be to God, said the boy, who has guided us to His religion, for we could never have been guided without His favor. Now tell me about the beginning of this creation and how it is composed. Is it a single creation, or one that differs from itself? For I see so much difference among people, in their opinions and in their passions.

The scholar said: As for the creation of bodies, it does differ, as you can see in the variety of tongues and colors. That variety is a proof of His power, made plain through His signs, so that created beings may know one another — a child knowing his father and a father his son, a man knowing his own wife and no other, a woman her own husband and no other. So God created them. But as for the creation of the instrument — that is, the senses, both what is visible of them and what is hidden — it is a single creation, and what is visible tells you about what is hidden. Have you ever seen a scholar with three eyes, so that his surplus of knowledge showed on him, or an ignorant man with a single eye, so that his lack showed on him — such that one might say the scholar saw because he had more and the ignorant man failed to see because he had less? Have you ever seen the outward instrument of one man exceed that of another? No — you see their creation as nothing but a single, even creation in the visible instrument, and the sense of the composition is one and the same. From this we know that the inner senses follow the very same pattern. This is justice. God would not be just in what is visible and unjust in what is hidden. He gave the scholar no second heart in one breast, nor did He rob the ignorant man of anything. The instrument is one, and the composition belongs to the One who gathered it. By this very thing God has argued against them — by the instrument He gave them and which they failed to use. The Almighty said:

> لَهُمْ قُلُوبٌ لَا يَفْقَهُونَ بِهَا وَلَهُمْ أَعْيُنٌ لَا يُبْصِرُونَ بِهَا وَلَهُمْ آذَانٌ لَا يَسْمَعُونَ بِهَا

They have hearts wherewith they do not understand, and they have eyes wherewith they do not see, and they have ears wherewith they do not hear.

Do you imagine that God, in His bounty and His generosity, laid upon them a charge they had no power to bear and carry? No. He is fairer than that.

The boy said: I see it no other way, and I would not claim otherwise. But I ask you about the difference of passions. Where did it come to them from, when the instrument is sound and the origin of the composition is one?

The scholar said: As for the origin, it is one. All of them descend from Adam, and Adam is from dust, created by his Lord, who breathed into him of His Spirit. But they departed from the Sunna in their marriages. They were born on a footing other than the religion and were raised in something other than guidance. And I do not doubt that among them are the children of fornication, who claim as fathers men who are not their own. When the roots were corrupted, the branches were corrupted with them and grew strange, and the return to the truth grew hard for them — all the harder for the arrogance that had entered them against obedience, the laziness against worship, and the envy of the friends of God, so that they no longer held themselves within what is lawful or held back from what is forbidden.

The boy said: If the origin is one and the instrument is one, where did the passions come to differ, when the aim in seeking is one — since every man seeks what is good for himself?

The scholar said: By my life, their aim in seeking is one, yet they differ in striking the mark, like archers aiming at a target. They agree in shooting at it with resolve and with the same instrument, and for all that they still differ in whether they hit it. So it is with the hearts within the breasts: they are gathered upon the minds, and the minds are gathered upon the safeguarding of the bodies and their dignity. When the call of truth came, they differed. Some judged that answering the Messengers and humbling themselves before them belonged to their own dignity and guarded them from folly. Others judged that denying the Messengers and setting themselves above obedience to them belonged to their own dignity and guarded them from the narrowness of worship. The origin was one — the pursuit of ease for the body and of dignity for the soul. So one party chose what the Messengers promised them of God's reward, even though in this world it was rare and hard to reach, for the sake of its lasting. And the other party chose from the pleasures of this world, even though they perish, for the sake of their being at hand, the ease of pursuing them, and the swiftness of their reward. The very hearts by which the first sought the bliss of the Hereafter were the same hearts by which the others sought the bliss of this world. Each looks to himself, and each supposes himself a sincere counselor to himself. So they came together in the seeking and differed in the striking. That is of the justice of God, of His generosity, and of the reach of His gift: to every seeker is given from Him what he sought. Whoever desires the reward of this world, We give him of it, and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We give him of it.

The boy said: The people of this world stand in classes within their world. Some are rich, above all labor, kings by the abundance of their wealth. Others are poor, in need of wealth, and they serve the rich to gain from them. Then does the bliss of this world gather them onto one level, so that they end up all alike in the evil of the outcome? Or is there for some of them a standing apart from the rest?

The scholar said: It is of the justice of God that He joins them one to another and does not separate them from their companions and the people of their affection. They are equal in His punishment, just as they were gathered together in His disobedience.

The boy said: And what of this religion which God has honored, and perfected, and was pleased with as a religion for Himself, and made binding upon His servants? Will He accept from them a part of it without the rest, so that they stand in classes as the people of this world do? Or will He accept it only from the one who brings it whole?

The scholar said: If the people of this world stand in classes within their world, then the people of religion stand in degrees within their religion. In justice, it is a duty that the Creator be worshipped with the fullness of what He willed. But His riches are great, and great too is their need of Him. His mercy was wide enough for them, and He knew that among them are the weak; so He accepted from them whatever came easily of sincere striving in work and of effort spent in obedience, whether little or much of it. Then He charged each one with knowledge according to his strength and his deed, and gave every man of merit his due of merit, so that they stand in degrees with their Lord. Then, by His justice, He appointed for them, as the fruit of their obedience, that He would join them to the people of the complete religion and the excellent deed among His servants. The Almighty said:

> وَمَنْ يُطِعِ اللهَ وَالرَّسُولَ فَأُولَئِكَ مَعَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمَ اللهُ عَلَيْهِمْ مِنَ النَّبِيِّينَ وَالصِّدِّيقِينَ وَالشُّهَدَاءِ وَالصَّالِحِينَ وَحَسُنَ أُولَئِكَ رَفِيقًا ذَلِكَ الفَضْلُ مِنَ اللهِ

And whoever obeys God and the Messenger, those are with the ones upon whom God has bestowed favor, of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are. That is the bounty from God.

This is granted them for the effort they spent in obedience. It is not that their deeds equal the deeds of the righteous, but it is a mercy from God to them, weak though they were and slight though their works were.

The boy said: Praise be to God, who has done this for them. Then is it to be feared for anyone that he be punished for something other than disobedience, even if his work was little?

The scholar said: God is more just than that.

The boy said: Is it to be hoped, then, for anyone to enter Paradise without works — like the insane and the young children?

The scholar said: That falls under the grace of God, His generosity, and the breadth of His mercy.

The boy said: Then what is the limit of effort in obedience and of sincere work at which God becomes bound to accept a man's excuse in all the rest?

The scholar said: The reach of his knowledge and the utmost of his strength.

The boy said: Then describe to me, in the duty of knowledge and of action, the goal of each, that I may measure myself against it. If I am able to reach the goal in what pleases my Lord, I press on. And if not, I halt at the limit of my strength, and God has the greater right to excuse me for what I fell short of. I am certain of the justice of God and safe from His wronging me, yet afraid of the evil of my own soul.

The scholar said: Do not be afraid where you are safe, and do not feel safe where you should be afraid. Strive for God in the work with your self and your wealth. For God is not pleased by what He hates, nor does He hate what pleases Him. He has hated unbelief for His creation, and He is pleased by thankfulness from His servants and by justice in their ruling, and He accepts nothing else. Truthfulness and faithfulness are His two gardens, and none is saved with Him except the people of truthfulness and faithfulness.

The boy said: Then make plain to me the goal of the work within myself, and what God has made binding upon me in it.

The scholar said: Obedience to God ennobles its people, however humble their origins, and the good deed is the crown of the one who does it. As for what is a duty upon you in your own self, it is to perform all the obligations and to shun all the forbidden things, for that is what sustains the religion and keeps the body pure. And the sum of what makes the pleasure of God binding for you and secures His acceptance of you is this: that you bring to another what you would love him to bring to you, and that you hold back from him what you would love him to hold back from you. In that is justice, and God is pleased with justice.

The boy said: Yes, this is the binding truth, and whoever does not do it has no share with God in anything. Then is there, in what you have mentioned, any room in a time of necessity?

The scholar said: God has made room in that for His servants, out of tenderness and mercy from Him. He said:

> فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ غَيْرَ بَاغٍ وَلَا عَادٍ فَلَا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ

Whoever is compelled, without willful transgression and without excess, there is no sin upon him.

The boy said: Praise be to God, who has laid upon His servants no hardship in the religion. I am resolved to guard what I have been commanded, and I seek the help of God in what He has ordered of me. Then what is the duty regarding my wealth, which you joined to my self when you told me, Work with your self and your wealth?

The scholar said: As for your wealth, it is whatever God has granted you of every kind of gain. Take it only from what is lawful, and spend it only in its rightful place.

The boy said: And what is the lawful source it is taken from, and what is the rightful place it is spent in?

The scholar said: Its lawful source is the wholesomeness of the gains in which you have wronged no one and which you have not mixed with falsehood. As for its rightful claim, it is its zakat: that you look to all that has come into your hand, whether little of it or much, and bring out a fifth of the best of it — the dearest of it to you — and deliver it to the one whose claim upon you is binding. At that, your wealth is purified by the alms, just as your body was purified by the work. The work is a shield, and the zakat is a cleansing, and he has prospered who purifies himself.

The boy said: I will do it, and I turn to God in repentance for what has passed. Then what is the work in what remains of the wealth?

The scholar said: You spend it upon yourself and your dependents with kindness. And if a surplus of it stays with you, relieve with it the people of need among your brothers, and give your kindness to everyone who turns to you seeking it, for the one who has no surplus is in need that another give to him. So be swift to every good and foremost in every act of bounty. This is the goal of the work — if you have the patience for it.

The boy said: Yes, I will be patient, and then patient again. And how should a man in great need not be patient toward the one who has no need of his work? Every needy man is patient, and every man given a favor gives thanks.

The scholar, gladdened by the boy's words, said: Praise be to God, who has granted you what is right in speech. I ask Him to help you to the completion of the deed, for that is the perfection of merit.

The boy said: I had been seeking, for myself, the merit of a favor from another man's hand, and now that the merit has at last become mine from my own hand, I was on the point of denying it to myself — and I find no one more treacherous to my soul than myself. So here is all my wealth, between your hands, in five shares. One share of it is its zakat. One share is expiation for what I have squandered. One share is thanksgiving to God for what I have come to know. One share is for the poor among my brothers. And one share you are to accept by your grace, that it may be a provision for you. Gather them all to yourself, for God will send the like of them in their place.

The narrator said: The scholar's heart went out to the boy when he saw how clearly his true worth had come to light, and what the trial had brought out of the praiseworthy character within him, so that his merit stood revealed and his conduct proved pure.

The scholar said, his tears running down: O my son, it is for the like of you that the scholars set out upon the road. It is for the like of you that the earth is held firm and the sky is kept aloft. It is for the like of you that the bonds of kinship are made plain, and for the like of you that the rain falls from the openings of the clouds. So rejoice, O my son, in what God has granted you and in the breast He has opened to Islam. Receive the good news of a light from your Lord and an opening close at hand. Accept God's gift to you and the good things of His favors upon you, with abundant work and noble thanks. As for my share of this wealth, I have no need of it. I came out from wealth and fled the trial of it, and it would be no act of piety, O my son, for you to turn me back to what I have come to hate. As for your brothers' share, let it remain with you. If they ask you for anything, hand it to them yourself, so that they may know your merit and give thanks for your kindness. As for the share of expiation, keep it by you until you come to know your sin. As for the share of thanksgiving, let it be a trust in your keeping for God until you reach your maturity and rise to the highest of what you have come to know. As for the share of zakat, that too is a trust in your keeping for the one to whom it belongs. So gather them all to yourself until you meet him, for he is the one who holds authority over you and on your behalf.

The boy said: Then who is this generous one you speak of, whose judgment you never overstep and whose command you never transgress?

The scholar said: He is the one whose right God has made binding upon me and upon all the believers, in whose hand are the keys of the gardens and the landmarks of the kingdom, whose palms are open wide.

By the light of Sinai he is the cause behind the signs, the one whose knowledge summons to the loftiest of ends. Through him your light is made complete; through him God brings your affair to its perfection; and at his hand you are blessed.

The boy said: Kindness such as this — to whom does it belong, and who are you yourself?

The scholar said: I am his son and one of his servants in good works, seeking his pleasure and shunning his displeasure.

The boy said: I think myself far from his good pleasure, and yet near enough that, had I never known of him, I would have had an excuse. Do I have an excuse, now that I know?

The scholar said: An excuse is granted only before one is exposed to such knowledge.

The boy said: Shall I speak, or shall I hold back?

The scholar said: Say what seems best to you.

The boy said: Should you not, at this very moment, take me by the hand to the door of his chamber, that I may enter, and to the house of light, that I may draw from it? This belongs to the full measure of the truthfulness that is binding upon you.

The scholar said: This is your due, but only with his leave and his decision.

Then the scholar took his leave of the boy and departed. The boy longed to press him further, but thought better of forcing the matter. The scholar went on until he reached the boy's greater father, and he described the boy to him and assured him that the boy now belonged to the company of the people of goodness and to the lineage of truthfulness. The father marveled at it.

He said: Bring this boy to me swiftly, for I hope he will be a door of mercy that God opens for the people of his age.

> **A note for the reader.** *In this account a teacher is also called the father of the one he guides, so "father" now carries three men: the Master's own elder father here, the Master himself when the boy speaks, and the Arab chief who fathered the boy.*

The scholar tarried only a little, then returned to the boy, and found his body in a different state from the one in which he had left him.

The scholar said: What is this I see in you, unlike the state in which I left you?

The boy said: And what is it you have noticed in me, may my father and mother be your ransom?

The scholar said: A weakness of body and a yellowness of color.

The boy said: That comes from a desolation that fell upon me after you left.

The scholar said: What is this desolation, and what has brought on this weakness?

The boy said: Your absence left me desolate, and the fear of some misfortune before I could meet you again weakened me.

The scholar said: God has known what is in your heart, and so has made the affliction light for you, and has cast into the heart of the one who has charge of you a mercy toward you. So take up your provisions for the journey, for through you I shall reach my hope, and I shall bring you to the door of your goal. There is no power except by God.

At this the boy was so overcome by joy and reverence that his soul all but left his body, until God, knowing his condition, took hold of him and returned it to him. When he came to himself, he said:

Praise be to God, who has never ceased to be merciful to the believers.

And he gave great thanks to his father, and reached up to his palms to kiss them, and to his feet. He rose at once and took up the traveling kit, and the two of them set out until they came to the greater scholar. They asked leave and were admitted. They entered, gave their greetings, and sat down at his invitation. When they had settled into the gathering, the boy said to his teacher: Teach me how to speak and how to ask for what I need.

The teacher said to him: It is not lawful for me to instruct you in anything while you are in this place, out of reverence for its master. For you are in the hands of one who knows your need and knows what you desire.

So the boy held back, and they remained with the scholar for a time, until he had brought the boy's affair to completion and perfected his guidance, and the boy reached the end of his hope and came to know what he possessed and what was asked of him. Then they took their leave and went out, the two of them keeping their counsel. They had spoken no words in the gathering save those of peace and good cheer, for the boy had turned yellow from the depth of his awe and could not speak. The Shaykh, the lord of the house, gave orders that the two be treated well and honored, and that whatever they needed be provided. He then went along with them to his house, and when he had brought them inside he greeted them and showed his gladness at their coming.

He said to the scholar — for the two of them were friends, and between them lay brotherhood and a long acquaintance: Brother, is this the boy we used to hear of?

He said: Yes, this is the one whose report has grown sweet in men's hearts, so that the mention of him has risen upon the tongues of the believers.

The boy said: Has the report of my story truly reached the friends of God, so that they speak of me in their gatherings?

The scholar said: Yes, my brother, so it is.

The boy said: Favors have gathered round me from every side, and bounties have overtaken me from every path. I do not know whom to thank, nor whom to repay.

Then they all sat together and talked through the night. When morning came, they asked leave to enter upon the Shaykh. Once they were admitted and had finished their greetings, the Shaykh gave them leave to sit, and they sat. Then the Shaykh began to speak.

He said: Praise be to God, who has opened with His light the hearts that were sealed, and unlocked with His justice what was closed against the seeker, and made remembrance easy by His craft, as a gentleness to His servants and a mercy from Him to those who long for Him. He has not burdened His creation with the full measure of what is due to Him, nor has He been content that they deny His blessings. Rather, out of His justice, He has charged them only with what they are not too weak to bear, so that the matter was set level between two extremes, and for that reason was called justice. He has spread His hands wide with bounty in kindness and grace, and has not disappointed one who calls upon Him, nor deprived one who keeps silent. His blessings overflow and His favors abound, neither reserved for the one who gives thanks for them, for the greatness of His reward, nor withheld from the one who is ungrateful for them, for the greatness of His punishment. He has held His blessings too noble to be stinted, and made His proofs too well established to be denied. He is too vast in His encompassing to be contained within existence, and too high in His evidences to be met with rejection. He is present without being bounded, and known without being described. Glory be to Him. How great is His gentleness to His creation, how merciful is His might toward His servants, how just is His rule for all His power, how near is He to His people for all His loftiness, how far above all illusions for all His nearness. So worship Him and give thanks to Him. To Him you shall return.

Then he said: Now to proceed. It is among the honors of minds that they be put to use in seeking, and among the fruits of seeking is finding, and among the marks of finding is the sweetness of what is found. Every sweet, fresh spring has a surface that is drunk and a depth that lies veiled. The one who seeks it never wearies of the thought that pursues it, and creation never reaches the end of its purpose. Its marks are truth, and the truth of the truth is an obligation, and from this it was named truth, for the establishing of its obligation. Whoever withholds from the truth what is due to it is a wrongdoer. Indeed, among the rights of thought is the purifying of hearts by good manners, and among the rights of good manners is the seeking of knowledge, and among the rights of knowledge is acting upon it, and among the rights of acting upon it is that it be kept pure by obedience to those charged with authority, and among the rights of obedience is that it be carried through in hardship and ease alike, in good fortune and in trial the same.

وما يُلقاها إلا الذين صبروا وما يُلقاها إلا ذو حظ عظيم

And none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune.

Then he turned his face toward the boy and said: O young man, you have been honored as an intimate come to visit, and greeted as a guest who has set his course here. So what is your name?

He said: Ubayd Allah (عُبيد الله, 'little servant of Allah'), son of Abd Allah (عبد الله, 'servant of Allah').

The Shaykh said: That is your description, and your report has already reached us.

The boy said: I am free, son of Abd Allah.

The Shaykh said: And who freed you from a master, that you should be free?

The boy said: This scholar freed me — and he pointed with his hand to the scholar who had summoned him.

The Shaykh said: Consider now: if this man were himself owned and possessed nothing of his own, would his freeing of you be valid?

The boy said: It would not be valid.

The Shaykh said: Then what is your name?

At this the boy bowed his head, at a loss for an answer.

The Shaykh said: O young man, how can a thing know that which has no name?

The boy said: Then I am one newly born to you — so name me.

The Shaykh said: That waits until seven days are complete.

The Shaykh said: For the honoring of the newborn.

The boy said: And if the newborn dies before the seven days are complete?

The Shaykh said: No harm comes to him. He is named after that.

The boy said: And this name by which you will name me — is it mine?

The Shaykh said: Would you then become one that is worshipped, though you were born?

The boy said: How, then, is the matter of it to be stated?

The Shaykh said: The name belongs to you, and you belong to the name. So do not step beyond your bound, and take your leave until your term.

So the boy rose in haste, in the goodness of his obedience, and made no reply, in the goodness of his manners. He went out, and his father went out with him, until they returned to their lodging. The owner of the house greeted them.

He said: How does this brother of ours stand concerning his need?

The scholar said to him: A promise has been made, and the one promised is thirsty, and the term is near.

So they stayed until the seventh day. Then they asked leave of the Shaykh, and when he had granted it, he ordered the boy to wash and to put on his purest garments. As the boy set about the preparation, his heart sensed that his need would be granted that day, and that this preparation he had been ordered to make pointed to some good that would follow it. When he had done what he was ordered, they all went out. The boy went out saying, A day of fortune, and a patron of fortune, repeating it over and over. Nothing moved him to this saying but the fullness of his joy and the depth of his longing to know what would bring him nearer to the pleasure of God. When they came in upon the Shaykh, they found that he had taken up the implements of his work. He greeted them with peace, and they returned the greeting.

Then he ordered the boy to draw near to him, and he drew near, and he brought him close, and he came close. And he began to speak of matters that no fancies had ever encompassed, that no pens had ever traced, that had never crossed the heart of any human being — matters not to be mentioned in the assemblies of preachers, nor spoken openly in the gatherings where books are read, for the greatness of their excellence, matters unveiled to none but their own people. And when he had discharged his duty toward him, and led him out of the wildernesses of his bewilderment to the very end of guidance, his path became pure and his drink became sweet, and he came to know his Lord. So he released his pilgrim state by magnifying the sanctities of God, took hold of the firm rope, circled the ancient House, completed his rites with remembrance, and fulfilled his pilgrimage by the greatest sign.

Then he and his father kept coming and going to the Shaykh, studying what he had been given, and the boy held fast to his perseverance. He never wearied of asking, so noble did he find it, nor was he ever sated with the answer, so sweet did he find it. And so they remained for a span of time, until the Shaykh knew that the boy's root had been watered and his branch had climbed high.

Then the boy said to the Shaykh, in thanks to Allah and to him: Praise be to Allah, who has made you worthy of this station, so that through you He revives a religion and puts an end to an ignorance, and who has made you a place of return for the people and a sanctuary for them. You are the gate of the people of heaven and the ascent of the people of the earth. From the light of your might the lights appeared, and from the pouring of your palm the rivers flowed. May you remain so, until the one who is pleased with you is made pleased.

The Shaykh said: As for you, may Allah bless you in what He has given you, and aid you by His enabling grace to guard what has come to you, and set you rightly to work in His will, and smooth your way with the light of His guidance, and open your breast with the keys of wisdom, and ennoble your affair with the path of the call, and perfect your excellence with the confirmations of response, and bring you, in obedience to Him, to the best of your hope in His good pleasure. I bid you farewell, my son, and I give you leave to go. Your parting grieves me, but three considerations have forced it upon us. The first is that we are setting out on a journey to another land. The second is your separation from your family through all this time, together with the burden you took upon yourself in leaving without your father's permission, for in him there is a heavy grief and a great anger that nothing will dispel but your return — yet I have hope for your father, if you are gentle with him. And the third is the duty of fulfilling the right of this grace that has reached you, for it is incumbent upon you to serve God by it and to call others to it.

The boy said: Your parting is a sorrow laid upon me, and your loss a diminishment of me. But your counsel is the more rightly guiding, your command the more binding, and your judgment the more sound. So lay upon me what you see fit, dismiss me when you will, and be gracious enough to send my father with me to my land, that I may lean upon him in my work and entrust all my affairs to him.

The Shaykh said: I shall do that, and I enjoin upon you the fear of Allah who created you, and the guarding of the trust you have taken upon yourself, and the safeguarding of your father, who raised you when you were small and toiled long over your affair, with his person and his wealth. So do not clothe him in the garments of disdain, nor set him upon the vehicles of ruin. Do not slight his name, nor turn your speech away from his remembrance, nor betray him in your city. And at the outset there is room enough for you.

The boy said: May Allah reward you, as a patron of grace, on behalf of every grateful one, with good; and may the Lord of abundance repay you for your shepherding of us, on a day when hands are too weak to repay you. I will keep your commandment. So do not cut off my share of the blessing of your supplication.

Then they rose, clasped hands, and embraced, and each bade his friend farewell, unable to hold himself together under the weight of the parting, able to speak only by gesture. Then they went their separate ways.

So the scholar and the boy set out together, and when they had drawn near to the boy's city, where his father was, the scholar said to the boy: "O my son, I have understood the will of the Shaykh, and you have not. Guidance lies only in his words. This is your city, and we have come to its edge. So sit with us here, off the road, for I wish to remind you of some of my concerns and to charge you with what you should do."

When they had sat down, the scholar said: "O my son, I know your father and his enmity toward the people of this matter. Added to it now is your going out with me and your absence from him without his leave and without his trust. I wish to honor your father's view by keeping some of these affairs concealed, so that you may return to him, and he may be at ease once more, and stay near us. And I hope, if you are gentle with him, that he will be closer than anyone else to what you desire. Your absence has worn him down, and his solitude has come to frighten him. Know, my son, that Allah has opened to you, for the least of your striving, what I did not suppose you would reach until a long stretch of time had passed. Allah has been good to you, so be good to yourself, and honor the one through whom Allah has honored you. We have thought well of you, and our hope in you has been great. So keep the trust your father entrusted to you, and stand firm in your affair. Piety and wary devotion are the mainstay of your religion and your work; thanksgiving and patience are an increase to your light. Ask of Allah the opening of your provision and the goodness of His granting you success."

Then the scholar said: "I commend to you six qualities: that you trust in Allah when you are resolved; that you speak with a ruling when you are called upon; that you do not grow angry when you are wronged; that you do not weary when you are slandered; that whoever answers your call to the good, you bear with him patiently; and that you keep for yourself the best of that to which you call others. For Allah will help you and open the way before you."

The boy said: "May Allah reward you with three goods: an imam whose case you have upheld and whose trust you have counseled well, and a dead man whose life you graced with your kindness. My heart is full, and my breast is packed with light and gladness at the greatness of what you have laid open to me. I do not know which of your words is the finer: the outward, which you arranged in its sequence, or the inward, whose meanings you expounded."

The scholar said: "Praise be to Allah, who has made His way easy for you, brought its far reaches near to you, and helped you to bear its weight. I take my leave of you now and turn away from you. Is there any need still left?"

The boy said: "The pillars of my needs are three: a need already fulfilled, a need I hope for, and a need I ask you to grant of your kindness."

The scholar said: "I have understood your three needs, and I answer you concerning what you have asked. As for the need already past, it is your life in knowledge after death. May Allah bless you with a life in it and grant you the best of what you intended. As for the need for which you hope, it is to act upon what you have come to know and to accept it when you are brought to account. May Allah bring that about for you by His mercy. As for the need you ask of me, it is as though you have desired an increase upon what you have heard."

The boy said: "There is no increase greater than your knowing what is within me. So grant of your kindness what you see fit."

The scholar said: "As for my knowing what is within you, none knows the unseen but Allah. But the believer sees by the light of Allah:

المؤمن ينظر بنور الله

the believer sees by the light of Allah. As for the increase, I will lay its matter out plainly for you and set you upon the foundations by which you are to work. You are to take all these things whose outward form I have described to you, and turn them into parables. Whatever among them is praiseworthy is a likeness of the truth and its people — its noblest for their noblest, its tokens pointing to them. And whatever among the parables is blameworthy, I have turned upon the enemies of the truth and its people — its greatest for their greatest, its least for their least, its tokens pointing to them. These are the foundations of the science upon which action turns. If you preserve them, you will have need of none besides them. And I commend to you the fear of the One who created you when you were nothing, and the keeping of His covenant, and the fulfillment of the right He has laid upon you and upon all His creation."

When he had finished his discourse, and brought him to his place of safety, and completed his nurture of him, he said: "O my son, take care of yourself, for I have a work other than you, and this is the parting between me and you."

At the mention of parting the boy gave a gasp so violent that he almost took his own life, his spirit near to taking flight and his soul near to leaving his body. Then he bent to kiss the scholar's feet and wiped their dust upon his cheeks, and bade him farewell and departed. The boy returned to his house, his heart torn from him in dread, unable to hold back a single word of his grief at parting from his elder father, and from the father who had been the cause of his grace, until his family and his neighbors grew afraid for him. He passed his day and his night restless with sorrow and alarm. Then his father came in upon him, in anger.

edits.chapter_key: homecoming, the father, and the debate with abu malik
edits.body_md:
The father said: "My son, is this how sons repay their fathers? I taught you only the best that a father can teach a child, yet you disowned neither yourself nor your beliefs until the day I grew old and this stranger appeared. You drew him in upon me, and you went over to his cause without ever consulting your parents. If what I held was true, then you have wronged me in the very depths of my soul, for you hid the truth from me. And if it was false, then you have disobeyed me and courted your own ruin — and whatever has overtaken him has now overtaken me through you."

The boy said: "My father, I have shown you nothing but tenderness and compassion. You raised me out of mercy, and you provided for me, preferring me over family and wealth. I have no wish to be so ungrateful to you in our own day that I would fail you in either of the two forms of gratitude I owe you."

The Shaykh said: "What is the difference between the two?"

The boy said: "Either you let me offer you my courtesies and kindnesses, since I am your son, whom you raised as a child and who guides us to Allah; or you give me leave to debate with you openly and to speak my mind, so that I am safe from your anger and can draw freely on your understanding."

The Shaykh said: "As for outward courtesy while our hearts differ within — that is a reproach standing between us. How long can an outward agreement hold when its foundations are at odds? I do not want it. But your debate and your candor — those you have. So say what seems best to you."

The boy said: "In these forty years I have stood with you, have you ever found me to be anything but one of two things? Either you are a scholar who has withheld from me the teaching I was owed — and then do not blame me if you forbid me to seek my salvation elsewhere — or you are unlearned, and so you are excused in my eyes, but you needed a man who was a stranger to me. I went ahead of you to him because of your age and your late years, for I have heard his words just as you have heard them, and I have seen what you have seen."

The boy's words tore at the Shaykh's heart, and he saw there was no escaping any of these arguments, and his eyes brimmed with tears. He said: "My son, the argument raised against me is yours to make. You would meet the same fate as I if you kept your affairs hidden from me. Hold this to my account: if it is true, I will accept honor from you for my own sake; and even if it is false, I have set it aside for your sake, out of compassion for you."

So they debated over many sittings and opened their hearts to one another at length, until they were guided to the straight path — living by the religion of Allah, upholding it, holding fast to it, calling others to it, and helping one another in it. Through them Allah revived many of His creatures. He sent the boy out into the world to preach, with his father's blessing, and to summon others to him; and the boy returned to them and became a means of their guidance. Allah blessed the people of that country through them and at their hands. Allah's command was carried out, and slander came to nothing.

The boy's name was Salih (صالح, 'the righteous'), and his father's name was al-Bakhtari (البختري). The two were honored, raised above others, and given high standing for the excellence of the manners they had acquired. Word of them spread through the land, and word of their religion with it, until it reached a party of people who clung to the old creed. Al-Bakhtari had long held influence among them, and they feared that his leaving their religion would cut it off from them. So they set out and gathered before one of their scholars, called Abd al-Jabbar Abu Malik (أبو مالك), whom they had named — for his scrupulousness, the depth of his forbearance, and his defense of his religion — "Kab al-Ahbar (كعب الأحبار)." Among them he stood eminent for his knowledge, his grasp of speech, and his discernment of opinions. When they came in to him,

they said: "Abu Malik, do you not see what the boy has gone over to?"

He said: "Which boy?"

They said: "Salih ibn al-Bakhtari."

He said: "And what has he gone over to?"

They said: "We are telling you that a stranger has come to the country, with fine speech and a doctrine he calls people to, and we do not know what it is. The boy went to him and went out with him, without his father's leave, and was gone for a time. Then he came back to his father speaking the stranger's words and calling to what the stranger called for. We are told that his father has taken up his view and backed him in it. We are grieved at what they have done, and at our own holding back from them, for three reasons. First: there was a kindness of his that ran to us on his father's account, along with all you know of the brotherhood in religion between us — and we fear estrangement after closeness, and we hate division after brotherhood. Second: if these people are upon the truth, then we have fallen short in following them in it and in helping them. Third: if they have gone astray in it, then we have fallen short in turning them back from it and in upholding the truth and its people. You are the head of our religion and one of our standards, and we have come to inform you and to seek your counsel, and we will not overstep your judgment."

Abu Malik said: "Go gently, for this speech of yours has alarmed me. You know that al-Bakhtari and his son were among those we counted among the people of forbearance and scrupulousness, and that they have rights over us and old favors to their credit. You have said about them what you have said, and you are, in my regard, among those who do not turn from truth to anything else, so that Allah has made you independent of that. This is news that has reached a people, and its proof has grown plain to them, so they have followed it and been content with it. We cannot rule them mistaken and so wrong them, nor rule them guided and so wrong ourselves by imitating them; nor can we say they have been deceived and so reject them without knowing them, for they stand nobler than that in our eyes. What we must do is look upon this news with a fair eye, in the light of justice, and with a steadfast mind. For it has been said:

> من تثبّت في الأمور لم يزل سلطانه محروزاً، ومن عجّل في أمره لم يأمن زلة قدمه

He who is steadfast in his affairs keeps his authority secure, and he who is hasty in his affair is not safe from a slip of the foot. For a breach in anything else admits of repair, and what has spoiled in it can be replaced — like a flaw in food, whose harm is slight and whose remedy is near. But a breach in religion is a grievous harm and a ruinous loss; its flaw cannot be mended, nor can anything be taken in its place — like a breach in the medicine itself, which neither frees its owner nor lets him restore his own soul. We have been told in this that the best of provisions are the treasures of the heart and the acquiring of manners, whose fruits and outcomes are praiseworthy; and among their fruits is the practice of forbearance. Forbearance is the crown of the learned; noble aims raise them by it to the summits of glory, and their merit is made plain in every place, along with the honor they win when their request comes easily. We have laid up for ourselves a share of that forbearance we borrowed, and something of the manners we acquired in the years now past — amid straitened means and hard demands. We bore that for the sake of its virtue, and we seek its aid against the disasters of affairs and the accidents of the ages. We cannot let it go to waste, and this is the very hour of our need for it, and of putting it to use in what has befallen us in this matter that has arisen among our brothers. There is no sense in leaving them and what they hold without laying it open with them and debating it, with the forbearance of the capable and the understanding of seekers — free of any doubt in what we ourselves hold, and free of any charge against these people that they have turned from the truth in heedlessness, for they stand nobler than that in our eyes, or that they have strayed into error, for such error is beneath them. Falsehood has no eminence for whose sake the plain truth should be abandoned. But reflect with me on the affair of these people, for it cannot escape one of three states. Either the people hold to what we know of religion, and this new thing among them is only an increase in manners, hadiths, and poetry — and people's speech is much; or the people have been granted an increase in what they hold of the religion, and they have delighted in it, and:

> والعلم ضالة كل مؤمن

Knowledge is the lost property of every believer, and an increase in knowledge is better than a loss of it; or the people have been given a guidance other than what they had — from the prophethood of a prophet who came to them with it and called them to it, and they followed it upon a clear proof. None of this can be ruled out of the command of Allah, nor will creation reach the limit of Allah's decree concerning them and His will for them, however hard they strive, for:

> وإن الله كل يوم هو في شأن

And Allah, every day, is upon some matter."

They said: "Abu Malik, we came to you with hearts full of rage against these people — ready to call them unbelievers and refute their view, to the point that we held their blood and their property lawful. But we have found our hearts humbled by your words, and by the way you have stood by their argument and defended them."

Abu Malik said: "This argument of mine is not for their sake; it is for the truth, that I might not betray it while it is unseen. I have stood by the truth's argument on its behalf when the one who would argue for it is absent. Nor is it a defense of them; rather I have defended myself and you against speaking falsehood and against hurling ourselves blindly into what we have not encompassed in knowledge. Otherwise we would be, in that, like the tyrants of the nations gone before, when their doctrines pleased them in their own forbearance and they rejoiced in the knowledge they had — until they supposed they had encompassed all that Allah had commanded and taught and willed of that for His creation. So they said Allah would send no messengers after their messengers, and they never imagined that beyond the knowledge they had reached lay any doctrine at all. They passed judgment upon Allah that He should cut off His argument from His creation and His deputies in His earth. Then they made the knowledge of Allah in His servants, and that for which He had sent His prophets and messengers, the measure of their own minds, so that whatever ran past it was, in their view, error. By that opinion they went astray and led many astray. By their own ruling they made lawful what Allah had forbidden, and by their own view they killed the prophets of Allah. I seek refuge for you in Allah, that you should follow the whims of a people who went astray before you. For men of intellect can be bent by whim toward any meaning, and lured away from every path — save the path of religion, for it is the more forgiving in the seeking, and its merit is not hidden."

They said: "Abu Malik, we do not oppose your command, and your counsel to us is not lost on us. We would not obey you at the outset of our affair only to differ with you at its close. You have pointed to the course and hinted at the demand. If you see fit, take us to these people, that we may lay open their doctrine with them and examine it. If it is right guidance, we will follow it; and if it is error, we will shun it."

Abu Malik said: "That is doubt on your part in what you hold, and the doubter knows neither his own right nor another's falsehood."

They said: "Then we hold firm to our truth and give the lie to whatever differs from it, whatever it may be."

Abu Malik said: "That is not how the meaning is sought, nor is guidance found by giving the lie."

They said: "How, then, is the demand to be made, if we neither give the lie to falsehood nor affirm the truth?"

Abu Malik said: "If you already know the truth and its acceptance, and know falsehood and how to give it the lie, then you are not among the seekers at all; you are among the learned in prophethood and guidance, who judge over the people of the world by revelation."

They said: "Then we are content with the truth we hold, and we do not doubt it, and we excuse ourselves from the burden of the demand."

Abu Malik said: "Are you not troubled that they should have merit over you in one respect, when by this you would grant them merit over you in many? Would you be content to stand, through need, in the stations of the seekers, only to stand, through ignorance, in the stations of those who sit idle?"

They said: "How has that come about in us, and what merit have they over us?"

Abu Malik said: "Their merit over you lies in knowing what you know, and in an increase of what you do not know. This is a matter that has come upon a people: if you do not seek them out over it, they will seek you out for it; and if you will not listen to it, they will strive against you in it — and so they will win the merit over you by precedence, by demand, and by striving. As for sitting back from the demand, that is ignorance through and through, and negligence, and a fault upon the learned man until he teaches, and upon the ignorant man until he learns."

They said, "O Abu Malik, you have met us with argument from every road, and every word of yours is sound. So open for us, out of your own judgment, a door through which we may act."

Abu Malik said, "To be conceited about one's own opinion is a kind of blindness, and to neglect the search is a kind of error. There is no fault in the searching itself for those who seek, but the seeker must first know the doorways of the search, so that he may seek the truth through the knowledge of how to seek. Whoever seeks the truth without knowing how is the quickest of all to call it a lie, because falsehood announces itself early by its showiness and by how readily it agrees with people's opinions, whereas the truth announces itself early by the hardship it brings and by how it runs against a man's desires. And no one gives up the pursuit of his own desire and bears patiently the first onset of hardship except the man with a sound heart."

They said, "Here a door has opened for us, in which you point us toward the knowledge of the search. Make plain to us, then, what that knowledge is, and what the sound heart is."

Abu Malik said, "As for the knowledge of the search, it is that you know yourself to be in need. And the man in need seeks what he needs with the humility of one who wants something, standing before the thing he is asking for. As for the sound heart, it is a heart that does not go on denying whatever comes to it, whatever that may be, until the truth becomes the thing that makes itself plain and shows its own worth, and falsehood becomes the thing that lays bare its own disgrace. Then the heart tells falsehood apart by its own intelligence, and takes the truth in by its own readiness to receive it."

They said, "We have been told that whoever stands at this station — neither affirming the truth nor rejecting falsehood — is a man ignorant in his conduct, since he neither knows the truth well enough to follow it nor knows falsehood well enough to avoid it."

Abu Malik said, "What you have reported, you have believed. But has such a man not, by your own reckoning, passed out of the class of liars and entered the class of the ignorant?"

They said, "Yes. To our minds he is ignorant, not a liar."

Abu Malik said, "The ignorant man is the more to be hoped for where good is concerned, and where the seeking of good is concerned. He seeks knowledge for his own sake; and if he does not, the learned seek it out for him — for ignorance is the condition creation is born into, and there is no shame in it for a man who seeks knowledge on account of that very ignorance. Lying, on the other hand, is the worst of goods to trade in. The liar takes no guidance from his lying, and he is never believed even in what is recorded against him."

They said, "You have made us certain of it. We have come to know the flaw in lying, and so we will never again deny a thing until we know it for what it truly is. And you have shown us the doorway of the request — the reverence that is born of need for the thing sought. Now: is this reverence and humility toward the thing sought to be shown after it has made its rightness plain, or before it has spoken at all?"

Abu Malik said, "Only before it speaks, so that by your reverence you may draw its answer out of it."

They said, "Then suppose we revere the thing sought until what it holds within is made clear, and its answer turns out to be error — what becomes of that reverence? Has it not been spent for nothing?"

Abu Malik said, "No. Rather it comes back as reverence toward God and as lowliness before His command, and its reward is yours even if the one before whom you humbled yourself did not deserve it. For the seeker has paid the debt owed to the request, though the debt owed to the truth was never paid to him. His case in this is like the case of a man who stands before some king to ask for a gift, and in his asking nothing lies open to him but reverence, soft words, and the pressing of his plea. If the king gives him some part of what he asked, the king has paid the debt of the favor, and there is a reward for him in what he gave. And if he gives nothing at all, the petitioner has still paid the debt of the asking through the gentleness of his request, and it is the withholding that has bound the one who refused. So it is with the seeker of knowledge: it falls to him to begin with reverence, humility, and patience under trial until he has paid the debt of the request; and after that, time will bring him whatever it brings."

They said, "This is the plain and open truth. Will you give us leave to go out to the people upon what you have counseled us, and to overstep nothing of what you have commanded?"

Abu Malik said, "I would never counsel you to a thing and then be stingy with my own self in it. Were it not that I feared the fault of turning you back from the path of God, I would have counseled you to hold back while I went on ahead of you to the good — claiming that honor for myself and preferring my own soul above every other soul. But we go together, and I hearten you with my own company, as an honor to you and in thanks for the good you have singled me out to share."

They said, "It is as though you had been waiting for this very affair before this day came."

He said, "For this thing in particular, no. But I have never ceased to await relief from God from every side, hoping for good along every road, turning my ear toward every man who speaks and seeking some increase from his words, whether he be in the right or in the wrong."

They said, "That one might gain increase from the words of a man in the right, we grant you. But how do you hope for increase from the words of a man in the wrong?"

Abu Malik said, "Truth added upon truth is light; and to know falsehood for what it is, from the mouth of the man in the wrong, is an increase in certainty. And the more certainty grows, the more the light of the heart grows with it. No one is saved in the sight of God but the people of certainty. I am rising now to go to the people. If you are resolved to rise with me, then look to yourselves: whoever knows of a sin in himself, let him repent to God; whoever carries a debt, let him render it to the one it is owed. Wash yourselves clean of every defilement, put on for the request the purest garments of resolve, and bring to the thing sought the intention of a man in need — for I myself am doing just this. Our going out is a going out to God. If He finds truthfulness in us, He will grant us success in reaching His truth; and if He finds in us mockery of the religion, He will turn us away from His signs by the smallest touch of abasement, vindicating His friend against those who mock."

They said, "Yes. We will do what you have commanded — within three days."

He said, "No."

They said, "Within two days, then?"

He said, "No — only within this one day of ours. If you do it, well and good; and if not, then I am going on."

They said, "Then we repent to God from every sin, and we render every debt, and we do what you have commanded. There is no strength save in God."

So they did this that very day, and they all went out together until they came to the gate of al-Bakhtari. When they had greeted him and were seated, Abu Malik said to al-Bakhtari, "O Abu Salih (أبا صالح, 'father of Salih'), how is your son Salih, and where is he?"

Al-Bakhtari said, "Salih today is my father, and I am the son of Salih; and Salih is with his Lord."

Abu Malik, supposing that Salih had died — for his father had said he was with his Lord — said,

> إنا لله وإنا إليه راجعون

"To God we belong, and to Him we return. Has Salih died?"

Al-Bakhtari said, "Salih has not died and never will die. He endures as long as time itself endures."

Abu Malik said, "Here are three matters whose meanings have been turned upside down: the son has become the father; the Lord is present here upon the earth, and this Lord has a servant from whom one is brought to Him; and a thing created for perishing has become everlasting. Alas for seekers, at the tangle of such speech! And behind all this, I suspect, lies a further wonder still."

Al-Bakhtari said, "O Abu Malik, come to your need, and be steady in your asking, for you are only at the beginning of the trial."

Abu Malik said, "You have spoken truly. The beginning of the truth is a trial. My need is a meeting with the righteous servant."

Al-Bakhtari said, "There is no way to that. But perhaps you mean my son, Salih?"

He said, "Yes."

He said, "That is by his leave."

So the old man rose in haste and went in to his son Salih, and told him of Abu Malik and his companions, and he rejoiced at the news, for he knew the excellence of their minds. He said, "O God, open for Your servants the hearing of their hearts, guide them by Your mercy to the proofs of what is sought, and widen our breasts with the light of Your hidden light." Then he passed his hand over his face, cleared the sitting-place for them, and gave word to his father to bring them in.

When they had come in to him, greeted him, and taken their seats — Abu Malik and those beneath him settling into their places in order of rank — Salih drew Abu Malik near and seated him close beside himself. The first thing Salih said was, "O Abu Malik, you have honored us with your visit and outrun us to the good by your generosity; yet the greater right was yours, that we should have visited you, to keep faith with your affection and to render the long-standing debt owed to you."

Abu Malik said, "When were you ever wanting in excellence, O Abu al-Khair (أبا الخير, 'father of the good')? You were forbearing with us when we were small, and generous to us once we were grown, and you became among us one who calls to the good and warns of its opposite. Your root is wholesome, your branch stands high, your work is pure — so joy be to you."

Salih said to him, "Have you come to me as one who suspects, O Kab al-Ahbar, or as one who merely imitates? Where is that complete mind and that fine forbearance I once knew in you?"

Abu Malik said to him, "Your standing is too high for suspicion, and the religion is too high for mere imitation."

Salih said to him, "Then how do you call me a warner, when the warner is a prophet, and the prophet is a proof set by God between Himself and His creation — a proof for them and against them alike? How can one be a proof for you who is not also a proof against you?"

Abu Malik said, "You have spoken truly; this is its due. We do not go about this on the strength of easy words; but we began with you by way of what is fairer. I judged truthfulness the fitter thing for a man who has set himself up as a veil for the religion and a champion for the truth, and who has thrown open its doors to those who seek. We have come to know the excellence of the request, and so we sought you out and set our hope upon you as the one sought. Come, then, to our need."

Salih said, "O Abu Malik, is not the man whose excellence you have come to know also a man whose right has become binding upon you?"

He said, "Yes, it is binding."

He said, "Then when you came to know the excellence of the request, did you also come to know its due?"

He said, "And what is its due?"

Salih said to him, "To know its several faces, and then to seek out from among them the one in which the truth becomes binding upon you."

Abu Malik said, "And what are its faces, and how many faces has it?"

Salih said to him, "The request has three faces: a seeker who knows, a seeker who is coming to know, and a seeker who is only beginning to acquaint himself. Which of the three are you?"

Abu Malik said, "I have need to know all three. How could I lay claim to a station I do not even know?"

Salih said to him, "Then how did you lay claim to being a seeker at all, when you do not know the faces of the request?"

Abu Malik said, "I did not know them; so make them plain to me."

Salih said, "Wealth is the treasure of the people of this world, and knowledge is the treasure of the people of the Hereafter. The seeking of wealth is of three kinds: a seeker who seeks what he already owns; a seeker who seeks a thing owed to him and due at a fixed term; and a seeker who seeks the gift of alms. In just the same way, the seeking of the religion and of the treasures of the Hereafter has three faces. The first is a seeker who knows, and he is the godly scholar, who seeks out the dead in their ignorance to bring them back to life with his knowledge. The second is a seeker who is coming to know, and he is the learner who has come to know some of the degrees of knowledge and now seeks its farthest reach and its end. The third is a seeker who is beginning to acquaint himself, and he is the ignorant man whom his own ignorance makes known, who knows nothing beyond the fact that he knows himself to be in need; and so he seeks out the scholars in order to learn. These are the three faces, and these the descriptions of the seekers."

Abu Malik said, "Yes. These are the faces of the request, in the religion and in the world alike. And I am the seeker who is beginning to acquaint himself — who knows nothing, yet has come to know that he is in need. So teach me."

He said, "Did you come to know it, or did you come to know it by sight?"

Abu Malik said, "And what is the difference between the two?"

Salih said, "Knowledge is report; direct knowing is eyewitness."

Abu Malik said, "This too is among the things a man has need to know."

Salih said, "As for report, that is the case of an ignorant man who does not know that he is ignorant until he meets a scholar, and the scholar informs him of his ignorance; then he knows, on the scholar's word, that he is an ignorant man in need of knowledge — and so his knowledge of his own ignorance came to him as report. As for the knowing of one's need and ignorance by direct sight, that is the man who has come to realize within his own mind that he is asked about a thing and does not know how its answer runs; his breast is straitened by the ignorance, and he hopes for no relief except through knowing the very thing he was ignorant of — and so his ignorance became a knowing arrived at through his own mind. Ignorance is want, and want is a straitness, and straitness is a severe need that drives creatures to seek out room to breathe; and that room is the room of knowledge, for knowledge is wide and spacious. By this I have come to know that you are in need."

Abu Malik said: "I find within myself everything you have described. I have come to know that I am in need — in severe want. Relieve my want, then, by your excellence."

Salih said: "I see you rushing to ask before you have made certain."

Abu Malik said: "Want hurried me on with its straitness, so I hurried; and I came to know how good it is to have room to breathe, so I went seeking it."

Salih said to him: "If want has hurried you, and you have come to know the excellence of that breadth, then how do you stand as to knowing the one you seek?"

Abu Malik said: "Your excellence was made plain to me, so I made my way to you; the meaning was hinted at, so I sought you out."

Salih said to him: "And from where was it made plain to you that it is I, and not you, who is known for breadth, that you should seek me? From where did you learn that I am the one sought, that you should come to me? No scholar versed in prophecy pointed you toward me, that you might learn from him; nor have you seen in me the confirmations that the proofs supply, that you might know. Do you not see that you rise to the asking on nothing better than the ease of imitation, and so wrong wisdom and wrong yourself — like a man who measures with the underside of the measure? If he does not level it off, he wrongs the one he owes; and if he does level it off, he wrongs himself. So it is with one who takes his knowledge by imitation: if he acts upon it, he earns no thanks; and if he abandons it, it is called unbelief. And you, in my judgment, are of too fine a mind for that."

Abu Malik said: "I know indeed that this is so. But I had hoped that the truth is a thing that establishes itself, and that I might spare you the trouble of making certain; for disputation breeds contention, and contention breeds rancor, since each opponent is out to gain the upper hand over the other. And when was the truth ever won by a man who has thrown himself into the defense of what is false?"

Salih said to him: "Excellent, what you have said. The truth does establish itself, by its own excellence and honor; and when quarreling grows large, it turns the heart away from what is worthier than the quarrel. Yet there is no abandoning the way the scholars have laid down, for they have said: no seed thrives in earth that has not first been sweetened for it, and no knowledge grows in hearts that argument has not first purified for it."

Abu Malik said: "Then bring forward whatever arguments you will. For the speech of wisdom is like a jewel: turn it, and its light shines out; leave it lying, and its excellence is still not hidden."

Salih said to him: "You have spoken truly — but only where there is no counterfeit of coated glass set beside the jewel; there, indeed, the jewel is not hidden. Yet when claims grow many, and the tyrants of the world contend over the religion until they dress it in what is not itself and coat it with the counterfeit before those who seek it, then it becomes binding on the seeker to put the jewel to the test, so that its excellence may be made plain and the coated thing, along with its people, laid bare."

Abu Malik said: "You have dealt fairly and given the truth its due. As for the counterfeit these people trade in, we came to know it and its flaws, and so we rejected it and held fast to this doctrine by which we came to recognize one another, and we said: here is the sound jewel of speech. We stood by it, and you agreed with us upon it, and together we all took hold of its rope. So if you have found in its substance a meaning finer than it — well, by my life, one jewel can be finer than another. Show me, then, the excellence of your jewel, by a test through which its worth is known. As for our jewel, we have come to know it and made it known; so tell us what you make of it."

Salih said to him: "As for your jewel, it was honored among us, ranked with the sound jewel, until we submitted it to the jewelers and the men of the mines. They pronounced it false and would not take it from us as a jewel, and said: this is coated glass. They showed us its flaws, and it fell out of the class of the jewel. For a jewel is exalted only by its preciousness, by the recognition the people of insight give its excellence, and by their competing for it, until its price climbs to every height. And once the jewelers have cast it down, who is left to prize it but them — who will take it thereafter save the people of delusion, who neither sell nor buy? So too with knowledge: it is not knowledge until it has been submitted to those who possess the knowledge of heaven. If they accept it, it is sound knowledge; if they do not, it is idle talk — and idle talk has no place in wisdom, nor do the wise accept it."

Abu Malik said: "And who are these who possess the knowledge of heaven, now that the prophets and the messengers are gone? For we know of none such in this age of ours, and the people have had no dealings with their like since revelation by the Books was cut off; the nations follow nothing now but the reports handed down. What, then, is your word on this?"

Salih answered him: "Any religion held to by way of the handed-down reports alone is not to be called a religion, for religion is one, upright, God's by His own right, and admits no disagreement within it. The reports, as you already know, are full of disagreement, each one giving the other the lie — and the religion of God is far too precious for that."

Abu Malik said: "But when they differ over a report, they fall back on the Books. Whatever agrees with the Books they accept; whatever contradicts them they call a lie."

Salih said to him: "And what stands in the Books only in general terms — who will make it particular for them? And what stands there in detail — who will trace it back to its principle for them? Which of them is to be trusted over what God has made lawful and what He has forbidden? I heard you on the day of the dispute, when a man in distress came to you and said, O Abu Malik, I swore an oath of divorce and then broke it. You said to him, Some people hold that she has left you and is not lawful to you until she marries another husband; and some hold that she is still your wife and is not made forbidden to you by a single pronouncement. The man said to you, Then which of the two am I to act upon? You said to him, Act upon whichever of the two you please. So he rose from beside you not knowing whether he was going home to what is lawful or to what is forbidden. Is this how a ruling is given in the religion of God? Is this how God's lawful and His forbidden are made known?"

Abu Malik said: "The sacred law of my age has been ruined, suspended, thrown into disorder, and we hold to nothing now but the name of religion. What, then, is the state of religion in your view?"

Salih said to him: "And what is religion, O Abu Malik?"

He said: "Command and prohibition; the lawful and the forbidden; the sunnahs and the obligations."

Salih said to him: "And what, in your view, is the sacred law, if not this?"

Abu Malik said: "I know of nothing beyond what I have just described to you."

Salih said to him: "Then you have set religion and the sacred law together on a single ground?"

He said: "Yes."

Salih said to him: "Then religion has been thrown into disorder by the suspension of the law, and ruined by its ruin. What is left to you?"

Abu Malik held back from answering for a while, his head bowed, turning over the matter of his religion. Then he raised his head and said: "I do not see that anything is left to me. So what is religion in your view?"

Salih said to him: "Religion, in my view, has its veil drawn fast against the corrupters and its doors thrown open to the seekers. Noble is the one who reaches it first, and good attends the one who seeks it; through it works are honored, and through its justice the sacred laws come into flower. It is a bond joined from heaven to earth, unbroken and unsevered — the handhold of those who take hold, the rope of those who cling fast, the ark of tranquility, the ship of salvation, the light of life: noble in its content, safeguarded in its sciences, marked out in its jewels, its excellence hidden from none who look upon it."

Abu Malik said: "If God has a religion by which He will judge on the Day — one He is pleased with, one for which He rewards and punishes — then in that sense it exists. But now that it has been lost, its description has become clearer to me than the thing described. So how is it described?"

Salih said to him: "The good comes only from the good, O Abu Malik. Set your light in the lamp-niche of your intellect and grasp what is meant for you. The claims of what is decreed have pulled at you, the robes of arrogance have made you forget yourself, and you have taken upon your shoulders what none but you can bear — together with the affairs of these people who follow you in good faith, who have listened to your word, accepted your guidance, and trusted your judgment. It is your duty to shield yourself and them from a fire you cannot escape passing over; so seek the way to be saved from it. You are the most favored of them in God's grace, and the most bound to render Him thanks, for I have known you to recognize the good and to hope for its reward. As for what you asked — the establishing of that to which I have called you — it is my duty to prove it to you by whatever avenues you wish."

Abu Malik said: "Everything you have said up to this point is proven and true. As for the reports of the common people, religion is not made sound by them, and they are not fit for it. There remains for us only the knowledge of that to which you call us."

Salih said to him: "I call you to the justice of God and to His oneness."

Abu Malik said: "Excellent, that to which you call. Indeed, this very saying is what we hold, and we know its excellence above every other doctrine."

Salih said to him: "It is not where your fancy has run off to, O Abu Malik. The doctrine you mean is a describing of justice with no knowledge of the One so described, and a wandering among the names of God with no knowledge of His oneness. What I call you to is the knowledge of God's justice and the landmarks of His oneness. If you wish, I will halt you before the flaw in that saying at any point you please."

Abu Malik said: "If the doctrine of the people of justice is flawed, and their affirming of oneness a wandering, then there is no firm truth left upon the earth — unless the meaning be something other than all the doctrines. Show us, then, where the flaw in justice and oneness lies, and where it comes from."

Salih said to him: "Justice and oneness are among the noblest of all doctrines. Oneness is too great to be corrupted, for oneness has no opposite; and justice is not corrupted, for it is the judgment between God and His creation. But the doctrines are all corrupted by the way men have corrupted the saying of justice and the rest — for it is a claim by which no statement is proved, and they do not encompass the knowledge of what they have said until they defer to the command of God. So take up whichever of the two you wish, defend it, and make it your own, until I strip it from you by the proof of the truth."
