Abu Malik said: "I would not defend a saying I do not hold, nor one whose author has asked this of me; I have not set myself up as agent for his saying, nor am I a keeper over the authors of the doctrines. Before you I defend only my own saying. I say that God is One, that nothing is like Him (ليس كمثله شيء), just in His ruling, who lays upon His servants no burden they have no strength to bear. He commanded them and forbade them, yet He did not command by compulsion nor forbid by force; rather His command is a granting of choice, and His prohibition a warning — so that the obedient did not obey under coercion, and the disobedient did not disobey as men overpowered. This is my meaning, and this is what I hold."

Salih said to him: "Did I not tell you that this doctrine is among the noblest? But these are names and attributes that avail nothing unless their meaning is present. It is as when you say, fire is hot: you have spoken truly, yet the truth does you no good, for your saying fire is hot is a name and an attribute whose mere utterance avails nothing — no food is cooked by it, no darkness lit by it — apart from the meaning that fire actually exists. Were names and attributes to stand in things in the place of the meanings themselves, then the word fire would burn your tongue and the word food would fill you."

Abu Malik said: "As for the saying about these things, you have spoken truly, for their names and attributes avail nothing unless their meaning is present. So show me that my saying of justice and of oneness are names and attributes that require the knowledge of a named thing that is described."

Salih said to him: "Your saying that God is One: one (واحد) is four letters, and we see two of them joined and two of them apart. Which of them is the one? Or are all of them together the one? And your saying Allah is four letters: which of them is Allah? Or are all of them together Allah? Or are they signs pointing to God? Or do you say otherwise?"

Abu Malik bowed his head for a while, then said: "I find no way out of this except that they are signs pointing to God."

Salih said to him: "Which of them points to God? And by what do they point to Him—by standing apart or by being joined? Or by some standing alone while others are joined, as in your saying Allah, where the alif (الألف) stands alone and the three letters are connected? Which of them points to God: this one standing alone, or these joined together?"

Abu Malik said: "I do not know what to tell you about this. Take us on to another door."

Salih said to him: "Then the door to the knowledge of oneness has been closed before you, O Abu Malik, by whoever spoke to you in this way."

He said: "Yes."

Salih said to him: "Then let me ask you about your knowledge of God: where is it from, and from whom did you take it? Was it from an attribute that pointed you to One who is described?"

He said: "No."

Salih said: "Then from a name pointing to a named one?"

He said: "Yes."

Salih said: "And what is the name that pointed you to Him?"

He said: "Allah."

Salih said: "Is Allah a name, or the named?"

He said: "The named."

Salih said: "Then what is the name?"

He said: "Allah."

Salih said: "So Allah is a name for Allah."

He said: "Yes."

Salih said: "Then what is the difference between the name and the named? Which of the two do you worship—one of them, or both?"

Abu Malik was bewildered for a while, turning his answer over in his mind, and then said: "I find no way through this except that I have looked upon all the crafts, and every craft has its craftsman; and so I judged that this mighty creation has a Creator who resembles nothing of what He has created, just as craftsmen do not resemble the things they make."

Salih said to him: "O Abu Malik, you have carried us away from the first meaning. The narrowness you feel in the meaning of oneness has driven you to seek Him by analogy and to coin likenesses for Him, and God is far too exalted for that. For every made thing is made from some thing, yet God did not create things out of anything that existed before them. These craftsmen you speak of you know only because you watched some of them with your own eyes, how each one fashions his work; and so you passed judgment upon a making whose maker was hidden from you, drawing your conclusion by analogy from the like of it that you had seen among the craftsmen you have watched and known. But when God created, He did not make you a witness to the creation of what He made, nor was there for Him any like who makes as He makes; and yet you have testified by the like that is present to the like that is absent. I have never known you, O Abu Malik, to be satisfied with analogy in your religion; how then are you satisfied to seek the knowledge of your Lord by measurement? Your saying, nothing is like Him (ليس كمثله شيء), proves out of your own mouth that He has a likeness and that nothing is like that likeness. Had you meant oneness, you would have said, He is not like anything (ليس كهو شيء), and you would not have said, nothing is like Him (ليس كمثله شيء). Glory be to the One whom the reach of lofty resolves cannot seize by thought, and whom the straining of the pointing hand cannot attain by perception; rather He is exalted far above the description of those who are charged with duty. O Abu Malik, had you turned this quest toward one of His servants, or toward a king among His angels, you would have failed to grasp what might be said of him and how he was created—how then the One who created him? The lights of the people of the earth fall short of grasping the light of the sun, and the sun is but one of the lights of this world; so how shall the one who falls short of grasping a servant of His grasp the Creator? Say what seems right to you."

Abu Malik bowed long to the ground in his bewilderment, finding no path to speech.

Salih said to him: "O Abu Malik, raise your head and say what has come to you of speech."

Abu Malik said: "Speech is gone, and there is none; the minds are bewildered before the answer, the fancies are struck dumb before thought, and the instrument is too weak to grasp with it anything but seeking and asking."

Salih said: "O Abu Malik, One of such greatness—do the eyes grasp Him?"

He said: "No, He is higher than that."

Salih said: "Is speech heard from Him?"

He said: "There is no speech except from a speaker, and a speaker is described by his speech, and God is too great for attributes."

Salih said to him: "This Vast One of greatness, the High One of power—would He wrong His creation, charging them with what they cannot bear and commanding them with what they cannot grasp, and then punishing them if they fail to do it?"

Abu Malik said: "Whoever charges an obedient servant with what he has no strength to bear has charged him with disobedience, and to punish him for it is aggression, and God is far too exalted for that."

Salih said: "O Abu Malik, One so far above wrongdoing and too great for aggression—would He be content that ignorance should keep His servants company?"

Abu Malik said: "Ignorance is an outright denial of thanksgiving and a persisting in disbelief, and God loves none of the disbelievers."

Salih said: "Were they, then, created already knowing, aware of what is wanted of them?"

He said: "No, but He created them ignorant, knowing nothing."

Salih said: "Then from where do they come to know what He wants, so that it becomes binding upon them to please Him and to be guarded against His wrath?"

Abu Malik said that they had learned this from God.

Salih said: "If He is higher than sight can reach, wider than perception can grasp, and greater than the bounds of speech, then how does the one whom He commands and forbids come to know Him—so as to obey and not disobey, to give thanks and not deny—unless you grant that there are causes for this knowledge set between Him and His creation? Must there not be those who deliver His justice and bear witness to His witnessing, both for the servants and against them, whom He has chosen by His knowledge and singled out from all His creation, and made messengers to them and proofs against them, so that they stand as the just ones between Him and His servants, conveying His command and His prohibition, so that obedience to them is obedience to God and His good pleasure, and disobedience to them is His wrath and His punishment? For otherwise, how could the command reach creation from God?"

Abu Malik said: "This, to my mind, belongs to the foundations of justice. Once creation stands in need of God's justice to be taught what He wants of them, and this comes by the hand of the righteous one He has appointed, then each shall thank his benefactor, be rewarded by Him as He wills, be reproached by Him, and be punished by Him if He wills."

Salih said to him: "Is it permissible to rule with justice in any way other than this?"

He said: "It is permissible for none but God, and God is the wisest of judges."

Salih said: "Would it be permissible in His judgment that He lay a charge upon some of His creation and guide them to it through one of His just ones, and then lay that very same charge upon others, yet not guide them to it through one of His just ones as He guided the first?"

Abu Malik said: "The judgment can only be one, because justice is one. Were the ruling split into two meanings, one of the two would inevitably fall into wrong."

Salih said to him: "Has it not been established for you, then, that the judgment of God is one, that there is no difference within it, and that His way is one, unaltered from messenger to messenger? Were it not for the succession of the messengers and the standing of the command and the prohibition, the Truth would have no growth and creation no meaning."

He said: "Yes, this is the truth."

Salih said: "And is not this succession of theirs from God to His creation appointed so that He may make obedience binding upon them and impose it as a duty, and so that He may set them as an authority between Himself and His creatures—to bear witness for those who obey them, and so accept them, and to bear witness against those who disobey them, and so turn away from them?"

Abu Malik said: "The judgment could not have been otherwise; else He would have belied His messengers and broken His promise, and God is far too generous for that. The affair of the messengers has made it plain that they are of His justice, and that the servants worship Him by obeying them. But tell me of the ranks of these just ones before God: are they equal, or do some of them hold a merit above others?"

Salih said to him: "How could they be equal in rank when they are bound to render obedience one to another? Were they equal in rank, none of them would obey another. Rather, by His justice He has preferred some of them above others, so that obedience may pass from the lesser to the greater, and from the greater to one greater still, until obedience and worship reach through them the utmost limit that God has willed."

Abu Malik said: "And are the one who obeys the virtuous one among them and the virtuous one himself equal in reward?"

He said: "Yes; this belongs to the justice of God, which makes the due reward binding for every obedient servant, and one is not questioned about the rank of a virtuous one or a lesser one."

Abu Malik said: "Can anyone resemble the virtuous ones?"

He said: "That cannot be, because they come from the Creator bearing the knowledge of the unseen in the Books He has sent down to them, and none is able to bring the like of it except from God."

He said: "Then can anyone imitate the lesser one among them, since no Book is sent down to him in which knowledge of the unseen is revealed?"

He said: "No one is able to lay claim to that station."

He said: "And how is that, when they did not set forth the seven creations of the unseen as the virtuous one himself set them forth?"

Salih said to him: "If the virtuous one has set himself apart from others by the knowledge of the unseen in the revelation sent down, then the lesser one likewise has set himself apart from others by the knowledge of the unseen in the interpretation. Both its sending down and its interpretation are from God, and what is with God is attained only through inspiration."

Abu Malik said: "And is the lesser one also inspired?"

He said: "Yes, and for that very reason obedience to him became obedience to God."

Abu Malik said: "If you set him level with the virtuous one in obedience and in inspiration, why then do you call him the lesser one?"

Salih said: "By reason of his obedience to the virtuous one and his need of him."

Abu Malik said: "And what need has he of the creature, when the inspiration reaches him from the Creator?"

Salih said to him: "Even though the inspiration reaches him, it comes bearing the interpretation of the reports and the Books, and the remainder of what the virtuous ones have left behind—as it was revealed to Lot at the hands of Abraham, so that Abraham's merit was made plain; and as it was revealed to Ishmael and to Isaac, so that the goodness, the blessings, and the merit accrued to Abraham. Thus the inspiration from God is joined to His just ones upon His earth, each according to the measure of his rank. In His justice, He does not will to cut off His command, His prohibition, and His worship from His servants after He has favored them with it; for then worship would be severed and ignorance made lawful."

Abu Malik said: "The bearer of the revelation has shown his truthfulness by the knowledge of the unseen that is in his Book. By what, then, does the bearer of the interpretation show that the knowledge of the unseen is with him, so that the revelation bears witness for him and makes obedience to him uniquely binding, as it did for the bearer of the revelation?"

Salih said to him: "He comes in his interpretation with knowledge from heaven and a declaration from the highest assembly, and the Book bears witness to it."

Abu Malik said: "Then I bear witness to what the Books have borne witness to: that every interpretation to which the revelation testifies is a revelation from God; and otherwise the Books and the messengers would all have to be belied, since their meaning is one."

Then he said to him: "If some of them give the lie to others, all must be reckoned liars; and if some of them confirm others, all must be confirmed."

Abu Malik said to him: "Such is justice; by it the truthfulness is known, and the merit of the one who confirms it. He has made obedience binding to the possessors of firm resolve among the messengers, who are His just ones among His creation, and He charged them with conveying His message. If, then, obedience is binding by prophethood, by the revelation, and by the interpretation, what of these who sit in their councils in imitation of them, yet are not of them? They have all agreed that after their prophet there is no prophet, and no warner in their time, and that they themselves are the upholders of the command of God and of His religion, and that this saying of theirs leads to God's reward or His punishment. Yet you say otherwise. How, then, could the scholars of this community have neglected to look into this age?"

Salih said to him: "They have not left it wholly untouched, but they have not looked into it with a consideration that would set them right, nor has anyone spoken to them of it so that they might incline to it with their minds; for it has been made to soak into their hearts that they are the worthiest of the command of God and His religion, and that there is no prophet after their prophet—just as those said who came before them among the seducers of the bygone nations. So every nation has claimed that there is no prophet after its own prophet."

Abu Malik said: "And what was the beginning of that, and what did they intend by it?"

Salih answered him: "It began, in every age, with three men: a rebellious devil, a stubborn tyrant, and a dissembling jurist. By the saying they spread, they meant to sever the traces of the prophets from every mark of prophethood, and to turn prophethood itself into a dominion passed round among their own. They could not manage this until they had made the hearts of the nations drink in a single claim, pressed upon every nation alike: that God has sent no one better than your prophet, and that after him there is no prophet and no warner. So they whispered to them from a quarter they never perceived, and turned them from a direction they never knew. Each nation clung to its own prophet by denying whoever came after him, imagining that this brought it nearer to that prophet; and each nation branded every prophet after its own a liar. In this way the mention of prophethood and the traces of the prophets were cut off from all the nations together, so that they neither sought what they had lost, nor would have believed had they sought it. Thus the seducing devils gained mastery over the misguided and led them astray; the tyrants gained the power to kill the prophets and killed them; and the doubt-sowers among the corrupt jurists preened themselves, and were destroyed and destroyed others. All of this because the hearts of creation would not incline toward the prophets when they appeared, nor seek them out once they were gone. Their despair of the prophets ran so deep that when the prophets called them plainly to the truth, they were called liars, and were killed in the midst of the people, and no one felt any anger at it.

"Consider the nation of the Magi, clinging to its tyranny, worshipping its idols, keeping vigil over its fires, claiming that God will never send a messenger after their messenger. Consider the nation of the Torah, clinging to its scripture, bowed over its calf, standing by the bounds its prophets set, humbling itself before its Lord of judgment, claiming that God will never raise a messenger after Moses. Consider the nation of the Gospel, speaking in its similitudes, claiming that its prophet is its God, seeking nearness through its crosses, exalting its rabbis, saying that God will send no messenger after Jesus. And consider your own community: it has been led along the paths of those before it, and whoever strayed has drawn it into his straying; so it inherited the Book from other than its rightful people, walked with the religion along a way not its own, followed its great ones into error, obeyed its masters in misguidance, and its jurists abased themselves before the tyrants—until they set up for the people a religion other than the received practice, praying at other than its time and giving the alms otherwise than by its right. They stand banded together, patient with these masters, unwavering in their need of them, certain that they have no need of anyone else, saying that God will send no messenger and no warner after their Messenger. So you and your like followed the word of the great multitude, won over by the sheer weight of consensus and the coercion of the rulers. You accepted it from them, dressed it in the elegance of your doctrines, gave it preference by the fineness of your phrasing, and raised upon it an argument from justice so tight that no argument can be raised against you. So you stood forth, propped up from above by the mighty for the sake of prestige, while those below followed you out of appetite, all of them supposing this was the truth. But if this community must indeed be believed in what it has decreed against God—that His proofs have been cut off from His creation by a single thread of consensus—then the nations of old are the worthier to be believed, for they hold three qualities by which the argument stands against you, and by which the truth is theirs rather than yours."

Abu Malik said: "And what are those qualities in which their merit over us runs so high that their confirmation becomes binding if their saying is true, or their denial binding if their saying is crooked?"

Salih answered him: "Their saying is like yours, and yours is of the same stamp as theirs; your hearts have grown to resemble one another. And yet the merit in the argument is theirs over you. The first quality: they say they came to the religion of God before you, so theirs is the merit of the foremost. The second: the consensus, both theirs and yours, rests upon confirming what is with them, so theirs is the merit of the truthful. The third: your own testimony on their behalf, that their prophets are truthful and are the messengers of God—while not one of them has testified for your prophet, neither to prophethood nor to truthfulness. So the merit is theirs over you, by your own agreement with them together with their standing apart from you; for they say that whatever knowledge you possess is copied from theirs, and that theirs is the root of yours. This is their argument against you, clear in speech and plain in its justice. If, then, the ruling of creation is binding upon the Creator, the ruling of these people is the more binding still. But if it is the Creator who rules over His creation, abrogating what He wills and confirming what He wills, with none to overturn His ruling, then—by my life—the saying of all of them falls away, and the Creator stands foremost over creation and over the command, and every day He is engaged in some affair:

كل يوم هو في شأن

Every day He is engaged in some affair.

His act is not to be denied, though He should send a warner every single day."

Abu Malik said: "This community has folded itself into a far-reaching misguidance."

Salih answered him: "Most of the ancients went astray before them; for they cast off the friends of God, stripped them of their right, and let their own fools master their affair. They made lawful what God had forbidden, and did so deliberately, lest anything come to resemble prophethood and set the people longing for the prophets—and lest, when that longing came, they should hesitate to kill them. Instead they distracted the people with sovereignty and largesse, and drew them along in step with their own whims. In this they were helped by men known outwardly for truthfulness and piety, parading themselves before the people, until the very one who had commanded the community to the good turned it from the good, and the very one who had forbidden it the wrong pointed it toward the wrong; and those loyal to the friends of God grew few, so that truth and falsehood came round in turns, like light and darkness in their alternation. Were it not for the remnants of God's friends and His just ones in the earth, and the inspiration that comes to them, the little of truth would never prevail over the much of falsehood. For by what else would God set apart the foul from the good, if not by His just ones? And how would the argument of God reach the whole of creation, if not through them?"

Abu Malik said: "There is no way, and no escape, for the justice of God and His command, amid the throng of His adversaries, save through the just ones of God; and by them the argument from God to His creation is made sound."

Salih answered him: "Then, once it is established that the company of the prophets of God are the just ones, is not each single one of them called just?"

He said: "Indeed, he is a just one, as it is said:

شهد فلان وهو عدل من العدول

So-and-so testified, and he was one of the just."

Salih said to him: "Then it is settled for you that the just one is the friend of God, and that this has passed beyond your saying of mere attribution, so that he has become one who is himself described?"

He said: "Yes, that holds as a saying."

Salih said to him: "And whoever does not reach the one who is described, does the description profit him?"

He said: "The description does not profit him except by reaching the one who is described."

For whoever fell short of him could take no comfort in the description while the one described remained beyond his reach.

Salih said: "Then whoever does not know the just one of Allah and His guardian—will his speech be just?"

The narrator said: Abu Malik smiled and said: "You have drawn me out of my own chapter on justice and monotheism, and nothing has drawn me out of it but the truth itself, in the clearest of arguments and the gentlest of speech. After this, what chapter is left to prove?"

Salih said to him: "From here, O Abu Malik, the counterfeit glass falls away from those who trade in the colors of jewels. They could never tell its worth; but set it before those who know the gem, and it is exposed, and those they deceived are exposed along with it."

Abu Malik said: "I have believed, and I have acted upon it. But how are we to be kept safe from the nations that lead astray, and how are we to know the causes of Allah—or even one cause among them—when we never reach them in their own time, and in ours there is neither prophet nor messenger, as there was among the nations before us?"

Salih answered him: "Glory be to Allah, O Abu Malik. For a stretch of your life you have not ceased to speak of the justice of Allah, yet the moment We reasoned with you to establish it for you where it binds you, you turned back to speak of tyranny toward Allah, and to charge Him with injustice."

Abu Malik said: "Allah forbid. I do not say that, for whoever says it has transgressed and forged a lie against Allah. From where have you bound me to it?"

Salih said: "From your own saying that the age of the prophets has passed you by, and that in this time of ours there is neither prophet nor messenger. Was the sending of those in the first ages a justice from Him toward His servants, or was it in vain?"

He said: "Allah forbid that it be anything but justice from Him."

Salih said: "Then what has taken us out of that justice? Are we not His servants as they were, a creation like their creation, bound in service as they were bound? Has He then dealt unjustly with us after His justice toward them, so that we who come after are excused? Or has His giving run dry in this time of ours, so that we cling to the bounty granted to them, and He is content to have that from us? Or has the way of Allah altered in our case after it stood firm in those before us, so that we should pronounce upon Allah that He has changed? Or is His justice a right owed to us and His judgment binding upon us, as His way was with those before us—since there is no altering the words of Allah, and none to reverse His judgment? And who deserves the name the just except the guardians of Allah? Who among all that Allah created is just, except the one Allah chose, so that by His command he became just? For this reason the ruling is called just, on account of the justness of the one who ruled by it; and the truth is called truthful, on account of the truthfulness of the one who uttered it."

Abu Malik said: "It can be no otherwise, and it is not for us to say of Allah anything but the truth. Yet we followed our speech to our own opinion, and ruled by the absence of the righteous from among us. If that is part of the ruling of Allah and His way with us—as was His way with those before us in the intervals between one messenger and the next, like the span that lay between the religion of Abraham and the time of Moses and the Torah, and the span that lay between the Torah and the time of Jesus and the Gospel—then we have stood upon that same footing, working through the interval, holding fast to the traditions and the way."

Salih answered him: "The religion of Allah is too precious to Him for that. What interval was there after the religion of Abraham, when Allah sent after him Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Jonah, and Shuayb, leading on to Moses? He inspired them to the doing of good deeds, the call to the religion of Abraham, the establishment of the prayer according to its way, and the giving of the zakat according to its obligations, until the ruling of the Torah was sent down upon Moses. And what interval was there after the religion of Moses, between it and the Gospel, when Allah sent after Moses Joshua son of Nun, and Elias, Talut, David, Solomon, Zechariah, and John, leading on to Jesus? They upheld the ruling of the Torah, held to its religion, called to it and recited its Psalms, until the ruling of the Gospel was sent down upon Jesus. So it was with those who passed before them and those who came after, and the many generations between whom none knows but Allah. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, and to each Allah set forth parables, and each was called to the truth. Where, then, is this interval, and when was it? Allah Himself said,

عَلَى فَتْرَةٍ مِنَ الرُّسُل

after a succession of messengers—and so affirmed both the messengers and the interval together. The interval fell upon the rising of the call after fear, so that they called in secret and concealment. Why, then, would they be cut off from the earth? The earth is not left, for the blink of an eye, without the just one of Allah—either present and manifest, or in fear and veiled."

Abu Malik said: "This is a statement that cannot be turned back, a word set beyond doubt. As for the establishing of the proof of Allah through justice and the succession of messengers, that has been settled and made plain. What, then, is the meaning of their absence in this time of ours? What is its cause?"

Salih said to him: "And what was the cause of Moses's absence, when he went out from the city of Pharaoh and passed beyond it in fear and watchfulness, until he reached the land of Shuayb?"

Abu Malik said: "He fled from Pharaoh's people, hiding himself from them, for he feared for his life once they had agreed to kill him."

Salih said to him: "Have you heard, in this law of yours, of a single one of the just—the just of Allah, the sons of His prophets—who was killed for the sake of the religion and bore it in patience?"

Abu Malik said: "Yes. A great many of them have been killed."

Salih said to him: "Then which of the just of Allah would you have appear to you and to the people of your time? One who was killed, whom Allah raises up and sends back to you after death? Or one fleeing from your midst, whom you would drive back to the killing he escaped—when he has walked the way of Allah in His prophets and messengers, patient under fear and in hiding, until Allah judges between him and us, and He is the best of judges?"

Abu Malik said: "There is no blame on one who walks the way of the righteous, fearing for his life and fleeing his people. The blame falls on the wicked nations and the helpers of the powers of darkness, for killing the prophets of Allah and His just ones, and for banding together to do it."

Salih said: "Then what do you say of one who kills the just of Allah and His proof? Where does he end, and where ends the one who helped him?"

Abu Malik said: "In the Fire—and with him whoever blackened an ink for them or dipped a pen in their cause."

Salih said to him: "And what do your jurists say of this?"

Abu Malik said: "They call for mercy upon the slain, yet they find no disobedience in the killer."

Salih said to him: "And whoever obeys the killer of his own free will—is he not a partner with him in the blood of the slain?"

Abu Malik said: "Yes, by Allah. He is his partner, and worse than he."

Salih said to him: "His partnership is plain from his aiding him. But how did he become worse than he?"

Abu Malik said: "Were it not for the rulings the jurists hand down, the kingship of the tyrants could never have stood upon the shoulders of fools."

Salih said to him: "You have spoken the truth, O Abu Malik. Have you, then, been content to make their kingship your home, their land your dwelling, their soldiers your neighbors, and their guardsmen your close companions—while you are their just one, judging for them by your knowledge and settling your needs through their kingship? You called upon them in your petition and thanked them for what you sought. You crowned their tyranny with the crown of your justice, and they grew proud; you clothed their pride in the garment of the sacred law, and they went to excess; you lit up their falsehood by dimming your own truth. So the weak were misled by your example, and those scholars who were like you, and they said, These are the jurists of the community; in them we have a pattern to follow. You went astray by your own reasoning, and led others astray by the reasoning of the tyrants. You imagined the one called to account was someone other than yourselves, and you forgot the word of Allah, glory be to Him:

وَلاَ تَرْكَنُوْا إِلَى الذِيْنَ ظَلَمُوْا فَتَمَسَّكُمُ النَّارُ

And do not incline toward those who have done wrong, lest the Fire touch you. So you severed what Allah commanded to be joined, and you saw yourselves do it. You spoke of the outward forms of justice while straying from its path. You came upon His saying,

أَطِيْعُوْا اللهَ وَأَطِيْعُوْا الرَّسُوْلَ وَأَوْلِي الأَمْرِ مِنْكُمْ

Obey Allah, and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you, and you claimed that these powers of darkness were the ones in authority over you—though they disbelieve. And you forgot the word of Allah, exalted is He,

قَاتِلُوا الذِيْنَ يَلُونَكُمْ مِنَ الكُفَّار

Fight those of the disbelievers who are near you. So you disobeyed the one you were commanded to obey, and obeyed the one you were commanded to fight, all the while reckoning that you did well. Error carried you far, and opinion led you on, until you said that Allah will raise up in your age neither a messenger nor a warner. Is it that the goodness of your deeds has set you beyond need of Allah's guardians for the proof? Or that the ugliness of your deeds has cut off your hope of repentance to Allah? Or is it justice that you should pass judgment upon Allah without justice, and be content, on your Messenger's behalf, with what you would never accept for yourselves in his place? Would any one of you accept that his own child be killed, or that he be driven from his house and his property without right?"

Abu Malik said: "No one would accept that. Were any man's child killed, or he himself driven from his property, he would be enraged, and his people would be enraged for him, and they would not rest until he was satisfied."

Salih said to him: "Then Allah and His Messenger have the greater right that you be enraged for their anger, when His vicegerent is killed and His guardian is driven from the land."

Abu Malik said: "It weighs heavily upon us that the guardian of Allah should be killed among us or driven from his land. But they have deliberately kept themselves hidden from us, and the tyrants have gained the upper hand over us."

Salih said to him: "Had you supported the guardians of Allah, they would have appeared; had you forsaken His enemies, those enemies would not have prevailed. But the judgment binds you toward the guardians of Allah at three stations. There is the striker set in power, who never tires of the chase and is never satisfied even in triumph. There is the gloating one, well pleased, who bites his fingertips in rage, never slackening in his incitement against their enemy, never heedless of them even when they are heedless of him. And there is the one who hates the deed and holds fast to love for the guardians of Allah, yet forsakes them all the same—having no clear sight in faith and no trustworthiness to be relied upon in keeping a secret. For this the guardians of Allah have kept themselves hidden from you, by Taqiyya (تقيّة), out of caution before you and before this great mass who have taken their own desires for their god, flung themselves upon the goods of this world, and aided one another in killing the prophets. They were blind to the fault in their conduct, so they never called themselves to account for the injustice they did, nor humbled themselves to repent of what they had done. Instead they laid the injustice of their deeds upon Allah and ascribed it to Him, and they said, Allah will raise up, after their messenger, neither a messenger nor a warner. So they made lawful the killing of the guardians of Allah without right. They wronged in the deed, they swerved in the word, and they overstepped in their denial."

Abu Malik said: "Yes. This is the very likeness of this nation of ours, and this is what they say. Where, then, is the deliverance from it, and where is the escape from the punishment of Allah?"

Salih said to him: "To Allah. Seek refuge in Him, and He grants you refuge; turn to Him in repentance, and He accepts your repentance; ask Him for the way of His guardians, and by your deeds He delivers you from the deeds of those who have done wrong. So too with this mass of people: were they to repent to Allah, He would accept their repentance—and what then would Allah do by punishing them? For Allah wrongs them not by the weight of an atom, even when they are unjust and lie, nor does He rush them to punishment, even when they rush to disobey."

Abu Malik said: "Then I seek refuge from the punishment of Allah by repenting to Him and seeking the means to what pleases Him. Show favor to the one who seeks you, and to the one who asks to be led, by guiding him, and your Lord will reward you."

Salih said to him: "If you do that, you will find Allah nearer to pardoning you than you are to repenting to Him, for He loves those who turn to Him. And you will find me eager for your guidance, watchful over you."

Then Salih's eyes brimmed with tears at the mention of repentance, and the fullness of his feeling broke off his speech. He gave them heart and bade them go to his father's house. He went in to his father, the scholar who had first sent him out, and took counsel with him over the affair of Abu Malik and his companions.

The scholar said: "You know your companions best. If you find good in them, guide them with your guidance; and when you warn them, let no eagerness move you to impose tazir (تعزير) upon them. Test them by leaving them to themselves, without harshness, and bid your father be kind to them and deal righteously with them in due season. The one who inclines toward good is not hidden, and Allah will not abandon you behind your back. From the light of His enabling grace He will open for you that by which the affairs of His creation are set in order, and from the gates of guidance that by which He shows you the deeds of the rightly guided."

He said: So Abu Malik and his companions went back and forth under this testing until their affair was fulfilled and they came to know their own guidance, and the guardian of Allah among them inclined kindly toward guiding them. They gave thanks to Allah for that, and returned to their people as warners, and through them Allah guided a great many of His servants to His religion.

The author said: Whatever in this account took the shape of a narrative was no idle telling, but a confirmation of what Allah has commanded—for in it lies the steadfastness of the messengers, the signs of the guardians, and the manners of the seekers.

Praise be to Allah, first and last. May Allah bless His Messenger, our master Muhammad, sent forth from Him to His creation as a bearer of good tidings and a warner; and His guardian, the Imam of the God-fearing, the leader of the radiant and honored, the beloved of the Lord of the Worlds; and the Imams from the people of his house, upon whom Allah has bestowed His favor, from whom He has removed all defilement, and whom He has purified completely. Allah is sufficient for us, and how excellent a Trustee, how excellent a Master, and how excellent a Helper. There is no power and no strength except by Allah, the Most High, the Most Great.

> **Editorial note (source-grounded).** 
> Throughout this chapter the father is called "the Shaykh," a title the story keeps binding to
> his advanced years — "the day I grew old," "your age and your late years." The word repays a
> moment's attention: it grows from a root (sh-y-kh) meaning to grow old and become an elder, and
> it begins as simply "old man" before ripening into "master," the one whose accumulated years
> have become an authority worth following. That double sense sits quietly under the whole
> exchange. The son honors the aged man who raised him even as he questions the elder's teaching,
> and the father's own anguish — that his son went ahead of him "because of your age" — turns on
> the gap between the two meanings: an elder in years is not automatically a master in truth. The
> same title later attaches to Abu Malik, again for the standing his knowledge and forbearance had
> earned him.
